newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto suffers fresh legal blows.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto suffers fresh legal blows.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto suffered fresh blows on Thursday as her party's former chief ministers in two provinces gave up or lost legal battles for reinstatement days before scheduled elections.

Abdullah Shah of Bhutto's southern home province of Sindh withdrew a legal challenge to his sacking while the High Court in North West Frontier province upheld the dismissal of the pro-Bhutto chief minister Aftab Ahmad Sherapo.

The setbacks followed the Supreme Court's endorsement on Wednesday of President Farooq Leghari's November 5 removal of Bhutto's government for alleged corruption and misrule and his dissolution of the National Assembly (lower house).
All of Pakistan's four provincial assemblies were dissolved on similar grounds.
High Courts in the other two provinces, Punjab and Baluchistan, are yet to pronounce judgements on challenges to the sacking of provincial assemblies and governments there.
Pakistanis vote on Monday to elect new national and provincial assemblies.

An official of the Sindh High Court in Karachi, the provincial capital, said lawyers for Abdullah Shah, a member of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP), had withdrawn his case, meaning that he had accepted November's dissolution of the provincial legislature.

A five-judge bench of the Peshawar High Court in the North West Frontier ruled that the provincial governor's order on November 12 dissolving the local assembly and dismissing Sherpao's PPP-led cabinet was "constitutionally valid and unexceptionable", the official APP news agency said.

It quoted a brief verdict as saying the governor was "justified in forming the opinion that a situation had arisen in which the government of the province could not be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the constitution and an appeal to the electorate was necessary".
Bhutto called the 6-1 Supreme Court verdict by a seven-judge bench part of a plot to drive her from politics.

"They can't eliminate us politically. They want to eliminate us judicially," she told a news conference on Wednesday at her home in Karachi. She predicted the verdict would be followed by a crackdown on her Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
"Now they will form false murder charges against me and there would be a mass arrest of our workers," she said.
Opinion polls suggest she will lose the national elections to former prime minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML).

The latest, by Gallup Pakistan, said 40 percent of its respondents planned on voting for the PML and just 20 percent for the PPP, although it said Bhutto's party usually added five to 10 percentage points by election day.
Many analysts, however, say Sharif is unlikely to win an absolute majority of the 217 National Assembly seats and may have to look for a coalition partner.
Another main party in the elections is the Mohajir National Movement (MQM), which represents Moslems who crossed from India to Pakistan after the old British Raj was divided at independence in 1947.
It is likely to poll heavily in Sindh, where most of the so-called mohajirs settled.

Former Pakistani cricket captain Imran Khan, a widely revered figure in a country where cricket is the main national sport, is also in the race with his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement), but he is seen as unlikely to win many seats.
